name: NR and NMN
summary: Nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) are two different compounds involved in making NAD, a molecule cells use in metabolism. They are sold as supplements, often under the same marketing theme, but they are not interchangeable ingredients.
roles: NAD carries electrons in reactions that help cells process energy and is also used by enzymes involved in cell signaling.
Cells can convert NR into NMN, then NMN into NAD; sharing a pathway does not make the two supplements equivalent.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test. A research measurement of NAD is not a validated test of whether someone needs NR or NMN.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

forms.name: Nicotinamide riboside (NR)
forms.note: A nucleoside, often supplied as NR chloride. It is distinct from NMN and from nicotinamide, another NAD precursor.

forms.name: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN)
forms.note: A nucleotide with a phosphate group. Findings about an NR product cannot be transferred to an NMN product, or the reverse.

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA (2019) judged nicotinamide riboside chloride safe up to 300 mg a day for healthy adults, and up to 230 mg a day for pregnant and breastfeeding women. That is a novel-food safety assessment of NR chloride, not a tolerable upper intake level; the opinion cites an upper limit of 900 mg a day for nicotinamide. No EFSA opinion on NMN was read for this guide, so no amount is given for it.

cautions: The body using NAD does not establish that taking either precursor slows aging or improves health; this guide has not reviewed those claims.
Short-term tolerability findings do not establish safety over years. This guide does not establish long-term safety for either compound.
This combined page is for identifying ingredients, not combining their study results. Product form and the compound actually tested matter.

origin: NAD is a molecule found in every cell. Nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) are related to vitamin B3 and are building blocks that cells can turn into NAD.

Both are made in a factory for supplements. They occur naturally in foods only in tiny amounts, and NAD itself is reported to fall with age; whether topping it up helps health is what the studies test.
dosage: There is no reference intake and no upper limit for this ingredient. Studies have used different amounts of NR and NMN, and they cannot be compared by weight.
Amounts commonly used in studies and supplements are about 300 to 450 mg a day of NR or about 500 mg of NMN. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

Check whether the label names NR (often NR chloride) or NMN, and how much of the compound is in a serving. Short human trials have mostly looked at tolerability and blood NAD levels, not long-term safety.

foodAmounts.verdict: Not checked. Both compounds occur in foods such as milk, but only in small amounts, and this guide has no checked per-food figures, so it cannot say how much food would match the 300–500 mg commonly used in supplements.
foodAmounts.notChecked: The food table used by this app does not measure NR or NMN, so no amounts are listed.
